title: Stingrays

names.gloss: stingray; long ago only old people were allowed to eat it
small spotted stingray, 'looks like a butterfly flying through the water'
small species of stingray; also thunder

identification.basis: The dictionary has a dozen ray words including yawu 'stingray' with its eating rule; Anderson records the spearing of stingray at Bloomfield, its restrictions and its barbs; Roth describes the stingray-barbed spears and the trade in barbs.

summary: **[yawu](word:yawu)** is the stingray, and the dictionary's note on it is a rule: 'Long ago only old people were allowed to eat it, but now this isn't followed much. Spearing one will bring on thunder and rainstorms' [ref:hershberger1982]. The barb, the serrated spine from the tail, was the point of the war spear and the fishing spear across the coast: *dikarra* in the dictionary is 'war spear, has a stingray barb', and Roth describes the single- and multiple-barbed spears of the Bloomfield and the trade in barbs up the Palmer, 'rolled up in bark' in teatree parcels [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1909] [ref:roth1904]. The rays themselves are the estuary stingray of the mangrove creeks, the spotted and blue-spotted rays of the sand and reef, the shovelnose and the big mantas, each with its word [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray] [ref:hershberger1982]. Most of what is written about rays comes from the Eastern Kuku Yalanji coast; each place on this page says what is known there.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[yawu](word:yawu)** 'stingray. Long ago only old people were allowed to eat it, but now this isn't followed much. Spearing one will bring on thunder and rainstorms'. **[walbul-walbul](word:walbul-walbul)** 'small stingray, spotted. Looks like a butterfly flying through the water', a word that is also 'butterfly'. **[jarramali](word:jarramali)** 'small species of stingray', the same word as 'thunder, thunderstorm'. **[janbal](word:janbal)** 'blue spotted fantail ray'. **[badibu](word:badibu)** 'spotted eagle ray'. **[bilaji](word:bilaji)** 'flat-tailed ray'. **[ngarmu](word:ngarmu)** 'shovelnose ray'. **[walkan](word:walkan)** 'diamond fish, devil ray'. **[yalnganji](word:yalnganji)** 'manta ray (Yalanji)' and **[yidi](word:yidi)** '(Nyungkul)'. **[dikarra](word:dikarra)** 'war spear, has a stingray barb' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's Cape Bedford name for the stingray-barbed spear was *nin-lon*, 'probably connected with the Butcher's Hill KYE word *molluu*, stingaree'; the Bloomfield single-barb spear was *ta-chal* and the multiple-barb *dikara* [ref:roth1909].

sections.heading: The rays, the spearing and the barb
sections.body:
**The estuary stingray** (*Hemitrygon fluviorum*), 'also called the estuary stingaree or brown stingray', is the ray of the mangrove creeks of eastern Australia: 'a diamond-shaped pectoral fin disc about as wide as long', a wide triangular snout, a whip tail with the spine; 'while the estuary stingray has gained infamy for consuming farmed shellfish such as oysters, it mainly feeds on crustaceans and polychaete worms'; it bears live young, and is listed as vulnerable [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray]. The blue-spotted fantail ray, the eagle ray, the shovelnose and the mantas of the dictionary are the rays of the sand flats and the reef [ref:hershberger1982].

**The barb on the spear.** Roth: 'Stingaree-barbed, single or multiple with the barb or barbs pointing forwards, long proximal end of bamboo or reed, and short distal end of *Acacia* or *Drymophloeus normanbyi*, the local "black palm" ... On the Bloomfield the single-barb variety is known as *ta-chal*, but here the weapon is built of a short *Xanthorrhoea* butt, and long black-palm or blood-wood shaft.' The multiple-barbed spear 'with the barbs placed one behind the other, pointing backwards' was the Bloomfield *dikara* [ref:roth1909]. For carrying and trade, 'small articles ... e.g., pigments, stingaree-barbs' were rolled up in teatree bark, folded and tied with twine [ref:roth1904]. The [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera) page has the spears.

sections.heading: Telling the rays
sections.body:
- **Estuary stingray** (*yawu*): brown, diamond, whip-tailed, in the muddy creeks [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray].
- **Blue-spotted fantail ray** (*janbal*): small, round, bright blue spots, on the reef sand [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Spotted eagle ray** (*badibu*): pointed wings, a duck's snout, white spots, flying over the flats [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Shovelnose** (*ngarmu*): a shark's tail on a ray's head; no spine, and safe to handle by the tail [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Manta and devil rays** (*yalnganji*, *yidi*, *walkan*): the big ones of open water, no spine [ref:hershberger1982].
- **A butterfly in the water** is the small spotted ray, *walbul-walbul* [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **A ray's outline in the sand** at low tide where one has lain, and feeding pits in the flats [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray].
- **A cloud of mud** moving slowly in a creek shallow [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray].
- **Oyster beds bitten** [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray].
- **Thunder**: the dictionary's *jarramali* is both the small ray and the storm, and spearing *yawu* 'will bring on thunder and rainstorms' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Where they are
sections.body: The estuary stingray in the mangrove creeks and the tidal river; the spotted rays on the reef flats and sand at low tide; the eagle rays and mantas off the beaches and reefs [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray]. Inland, the freshwater whipray lives in some of the big rivers of the north; see the Hann River and upper Mitchell on this page, and the [sawfish and river sharks](entry:sawfish-and-river-sharks) page [ref:wiki-freshwater-whipray].

sections.heading: The ray on the flats
sections.body: The estuary stingray works the mud and the oyster beds for crabs and worms, and feeds the sharks and the people; on the Bloomfield it fed the spear-makers too, since every war spear and most fishing spears carried its spine [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray] [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1909]. The [mangroves](entry:mangroves) and the [mud crab](entry:mud-crab) pages have the flats it lives on.

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Speared on the reef and the flats at low tide through the dry; the rule that spearing one brings thunder sits oddly with the storm season, which is when the rays come up the creeks with the warm water [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Meat**, by the old rule for old people only [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996].
- **Barbs** for war and fishing spears, single or in rows; see [spears](entry:spear-and-woomera) [ref:roth1909] [ref:anderson1996].
- **Trade**: barbs and finished stingaree spears moved along the coast and inland to the Palmer and the Laura [ref:roth1909] [ref:roth1910].
- **Fat**: on the Batavia River stingray fat was boiled with bark into a cement [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Spearing a ray, and setting the barb
sections.body:
From Anderson and Roth [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1909]:

1. **Walk the reef flat or the creek bank at low tide**, or stand on an overhanging branch, with the multi-pronged [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera) [ref:anderson1996].
2. **Look for the outline in the sand** and the moving mud cloud [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray].
3. **Spear it through the disc** and keep clear of the tail; the spine strikes upward [ref:anderson1996].
4. **Cut the spine out** with the base intact; it is the barb [ref:roth1909].
5. **Set the barb** on the short hardwood or black-palm head of the spear with [sinew](entry:sinew) and [gum](entry:beeswax-and-gums), single and pointing forward for the *ta-chal*, several in a row pointing back for the *dikara* [ref:roth1909] [ref:anderson1996].
6. **Keep spare barbs** rolled in teatree bark and tied, the way they travelled in trade [ref:roth1904].
7. **The old rules**: adult men, not in front of a wife's brother, and the old people's meat; the dictionary says the eating rule 'isn't followed much' now, and leaves the rest [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- The spine is a serrated, venomous blade; a sting means hot water for the pain and a doctor for the wound, which can hold broken spine and infect [ref:isbister2007].
- Shuffle on the flats; a ray stepped on strikes.
- A barbed spear wound tears on the way out; the spear page says why [ref:roth1909].
- Creek flats are crocodile country; Be Crocwise [ref:crocwise].
- The estuary stingray is listed as vulnerable; take comes under the *Fisheries Act 1994* and, in sea country, the Traditional Owners' own plans [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray] [ref:qld-fishact].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The dictionary's dozen ray words are a field guide to a coast that has not been photographed under those names [ref:hershberger1982]. Who spears rays today, and where, is under each place on this page. The contribution box below is for the people who spear them.

locations.summary: **No ray is recorded on the Hann itself**: the Atlas of Living Australia holds no ray record in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann-fish]. Downstream, the North Kennedy and Normanby rivers in Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park are a breeding place of the **freshwater whipray**, 'the only Australian stingray confined to fresh and brackish waters' [ref:isra-normanby] [ref:wiki-freshwater-whipray]. A century ago the Koko-warra of the Normanby passed stingaree spears on in trade [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: The river's ray
sections.body: The freshwater whipray (*Urogymnus dalyensis*) is 'reported from the Daly, Fitzroy, Gilbert, Mitchell, Normanby, Ord, Pentecost, Roper, South Alligator, and Wenlock Rivers', 'typically reaching 1 m (3.3 ft) across', 'plain brown above and white below with dark marginal bands' [ref:wiki-freshwater-whipray]. It is told from the estuary stingray by living in fresh water.

sections.heading: Where it lives here
sections.body: The Normanby Catchment Important Shark and Ray Area 'includes the North Kennedy River to the west, the Bizant River, and the Normanby River to the east and part of the Laura River upstream'; the Hann flows into the North Kennedy [ref:isra-normanby] [ref:wp-hann]. There, 'between 2017–2025, 18 (14 with available size) Freshwater Whiprays ranging in size between 38–100 cm DW' were caught or reported, eight of them immature. The species 'appears to be highly resident, especially females' [ref:isra-normanby]. In a survey of Lakefield anglers in 1986–91, 'various sharks and rays' were caught in the estuarine habitats, not in fresh water [ref:russell1993]. Whether a whipray comes up the Hann is not recorded [ref:ala-hann-fish].

sections.heading: Its year here
sections.body: One 'likely pregnant female' was reported in June 2024 and a 'likely postpartum' female of 100 cm was caught in July 2024; the species is thought 'to give birth during the onset of the austral wet season (November to January)' [ref:isra-normanby]. That is when the Hann's flow starts to rise again from its September–November low [ref:bom-105001b].

sections.heading: How people used them here
sections.body: Roth recorded the stingaree spear moving through this country in trade. 'At Princess Charlotte Bay, the Koko-rarmul of the Morehead River give the Koko-warra (whose "country" extends along the course of the Normanby and Deighton Rivers) reed-spears, iron scraps, European tomahawks, etc., getting in return melo shell, grass-reed-spears, nautilus-shell necklaces; stingaree spears and fishing-nets.' People from the Endeavour and Bloomfield rivers travelled up towards the Laura River to supply the Koko-warra with red ochre, white clay and grass-tree spears, and were paid in the same goods [ref:roth1910]. Roth does not say where the barbs on those spears came from. Nothing else on rays is published for the Possum, Thaypan, Kuku Warra or Lama Lama peoples in the sources used here; the Uses section above has the rest.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: In Rinyirru 'recreational fishing is permitted at all camping areas' and 'Fisheries regulations apply' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-todo]. The whipray records come from Sharks And Rays Australia working with the Laura Rangers and the Rangers of Rinyirru Corporation [ref:isra-normanby]. The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan].

locations.summary: [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) is a long way from the sea country, and no ray is recorded there: the Atlas of Living Australia holds no shark or ray record within 60 km of the homestead [ref:ala-karma-60]. The barbs still came this way: Roth recorded them traded up the Palmer, and the words, the trade and the tools reach inland.

sections.heading: Where the nearest rays are
sections.body: On the Mitchell the freshwater whipray is a fish of the lower river: 'thirty-eight animals ranging in size between 59–138 cm disc width' were caught 'from ~13 km from the river mouth to more than ~17 km upstream' [ref:isra2025].

sections.heading: Barbs in trade
sections.body: Roth, on the stingaree-barbed spear: 'On the Middle Palmer the stingaree barbs are bartered into the district from the Musgrave River on the east coast, or from down the Mitchell, etc., on the Gulf coast' [ref:roth1909].

locations.summary: This is where the ray words and the rules come from: the dictionary was made on the Bloomfield [ref:hershberger1982], and Anderson's Bloomfield informants recorded who could spear a stingray, and when, and what it was for [ref:anderson1996]. Rays belong to the sea country of the Eastern Kuku Yalanji, the Bloomfield and Daintree coast.

sections.heading: Where they are here
sections.body: The estuary stingray in the mangrove creeks and the tidal river, the spotted rays on the reef flats and sand at low tide, the eagle rays and mantas off the beaches and reefs: all on the Bloomfield and Daintree coast [ref:wiki-estuary-stingray] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Spearing at the Bloomfield
sections.body:
At Bloomfield, spearing 'was normally men's work and it was done out on the reef at low tide, from the edges of a creek bank, in the water or while standing on an overhanging branch'; 'at other times rock cod, coral cod, red emperor, black-tip shark and stingrays were commonly speared. The latter species was important not only as a meat source, but for the supply of spear barbs. It is significant, too, that the spearing of stingray was surrounded by restrictions. Only adult men could obtain it, and even then never in the presence of, or with the knowledge of their wives' brothers (actual or classificatory). Multi-pronged spears were normally used' [ref:anderson1996].

At Bloomfield the barbs 'were held in place by wallaby [sinew](entry:sinew) and resins' [ref:anderson1996]. The Bloomfield people took in 'stingaree-spears' by barter [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Stingrays are still speared on the Bloomfield flats and still carry the only spear barb that grows [ref:anderson1996]. Sea-country take comes under the Traditional Owners' plan [ref:jabalbina2016].
